title: Draw the SN2 product with its stereochemistry
asks: A substrate with a stereocentre meets a good nucleophile. Draw the product, showing inversion.

know.h: {{SN2}} is concerted: the nucleophile bonds to carbon while the leaving group leaves, in one step with no intermediate. Rate = k[nucleophile][electrophile].

The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (backside attack). In the transition state the nucleophile, the carbon and the leaving group lie on one line, and the other three groups lie in one plane.
As the leaving group goes, the three other groups flip to the other side, like an umbrella in the wind. The result is inversion at the electrophilic carbon.

One enantiomer gives one enantiomer. The lecture example uses deuterium to make the carbon a stereocentre: [[rxn:[2H][C@H](C)Cl + [OH-]>>[2H][C@@H](C)O + [Cl-]]] (R)-1-chloro-1-deuterioethane gives (S)-1-deuterioethanol.
Deuterium (D) is an isotope of hydrogen. It is drawn as its own group and it ranks above H when you assign R or S, so a carbon carrying H, D and two other different groups is a stereocentre.

On a ring, a wedge becomes a dash. The lecture example (Walden inversion): 3-iodocyclohexanone with I on a wedge and NaSH give the thiol with SH on a dash. [[rxn:O=C1CCC[C@H](I)C1 + [SH-].[Na+]>>O=C1CCC[C@@H](S)C1 + [Na+].[I-]]]
If the ring has a second substituent, inversion at the attacked carbon turns cis into trans and trans into cis, because the other substituent stays where it was.
Only the carbon that loses the leaving group inverts. Every other stereocentre in the molecule keeps its wedge or dash.
know.from: Lecture 11/05, p. 1: inversion at the electrophile atom

know.h: Inversion describes the geometry. The R or S label usually changes too, but not always: the nucleophile may have a different priority from the leaving group. Draw the inverted product first, then assign R or S from scratch.

How to draw it: copy the skeleton, remove the leaving group, and put the nucleophile on the same carbon with the opposite kind of bond (wedge where the leaving group was dashed, dash where it was wedged).
{{SN2}} needs an open carbon: methyl (1) > primary (ethyl 0.033) > secondary (isopropyl 8.3 × 10<sup>-4</sup>) >>> tertiary (0, no {{SN2}}). A tertiary stereocentre does not give an inverted product.
Good leaving groups: {{I-}}, {{Br-}}, {{Cl-}} and tosylate ({{TsO-}}). In a tosylate the bond that breaks is the C-O bond: the whole OTs group leaves. {{HO-}} and {{F-}} are poor leaving groups.
Contrast with {{SN1}}: a planar carbocation is attacked on either face, which gives a racemic mixture. Inversion belongs to {{SN2}} only.

method: Find the leaving group and the carbon that carries it, and check that the carbon is methyl, primary or secondary (a tertiary carbon gives no SN2).
Find the atom of the nucleophile that attacks.
Copy the whole skeleton without the leaving group, leaving every other wedge and dash exactly as it was.
Attach the nucleophile to the carbon that lost the leaving group, on the opposite face: a wedge becomes a dash and a dash becomes a wedge.
On a ring, say whether the product is cis or trans. It is the opposite of the starting material.
If R or S is asked, assign it afresh on the product from the priorities of its four groups.
Write the leaving group as the by-product, with the counter-ion of the nucleophile.

pitfalls.h: Drawing the nucleophile on the same face the leaving group was on (retention).
Drawing both enantiomers or writing racemic. That is {{SN1}}, where a planar carbocation forms.
Flipping a stereocentre that was not attacked. Only the carbon that carried the leaving group changes.
Writing S for the product only because the starting material was R, without ranking the four groups again.
Leaving the oxygen of a tosylate on the carbon. The C-O bond breaks and the whole OTs group leaves.
Drawing an inverted product at a tertiary carbon, where {{SN2}} does not happen.
